title: The Deposition

jokes.text: Every time Michael's in a meeting, he makes me come in and give him a Post-it note telling him who's on the phone. I did it once and he freaked out. He loved it so much.
jokes.setup: Pam delivers a confessional explaining a workplace ritual that sounds like a normal executive assistant task
jokes.punchline: It only happened once by accident, and Michael loved it so much he institutionalized it as a recurring vanity performance
jokes.explanation: A tight, efficient cold-open joke that perfectly captures Michael's need to perform importance. The reveal that he has so few calls he needs fake ones is the real punchline buried inside. Strong character integration — this is completely Michael Scott behavior.

jokes.text: The thing is he doesn't get that many calls. So he has me make them up every 10 minutes.
jokes.setup: Pam has just explained Michael loves the Post-it ritual
jokes.punchline: The reason the ritual exists is because Michael receives so few real calls he requires fabricated ones to feel important
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'he loved the Post-it thing' to 'he gets so few real calls we fabricate them every 10 minutes' is the actual punchline of the cold open. Pam's deadpan delivery is everything. Excellent economy — maximum character reveal in minimum words.

jokes.text: No. Money isn't everything, Ryan. And you're my friend, and I don't want to be rude. / Take the call, friend. I refuse.
jokes.setup: Ryan, Michael's corporate superior, tells him to take the important client call; Michael performatively refuses to seem loyal
jokes.punchline: The elaborate back-and-forth of refusals and insistences reveals Michael is performing friendship theater for Ryan's benefit while ignoring actual business
jokes.explanation: Solid character comedy — Michael's need to perform warmth toward Ryan at the expense of actual work is very on-brand. The scene runs a beat too long, which dilutes the punch, but the dynamic is well-observed.

jokes.text: The company fired her for having the courage to augment her boobs.
jokes.setup: Michael is explaining Jan's wrongful termination lawsuit in earnest, legal-adjacent language
jokes.punchline: He reframes her breast augmentation surgery as an act of 'courage,' framing it as a civil rights matter
jokes.explanation: The word 'courage' is doing enormous heavy lifting here. Michael's complete sincerity — using heroic language for cosmetic surgery — is perfectly calibrated. Only Michael Scott would frame this with earnest moral indignation. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: "Pat-turn." My friend Pat took a turn. That's how I remember that.
jokes.setup: Michael is trying to memorize legal terminology ('pattern') for the deposition
jokes.punchline: His mnemonic device — imagining a friend named Pat taking a turn — is both useless as a memory tool and delivered with total confidence
jokes.explanation: This is exceptional character comedy. Michael's mnemonic devices are not just absurd — they are the kind of absurd that reveals he does not understand what mnemonics are for. 'Pat took a turn' tells you nothing about the word 'pattern,' which makes it funnier. His confidence is the engine. Scores near the episode's ceiling on character integration — this joke could only come from Michael Scott.

jokes.text: "Dis-ray." My friend Dis Ray got new specs.
jokes.setup: Michael continues his mnemonic system, now tackling 'disrespect'
jokes.punchline: 'Dis Ray' is a friend who got new glasses ('specs') — the mnemonic covers 'dis' and 'spec' but is so convoluted it's functionally useless
jokes.explanation: The running gag of Michael's mnemonics escalates here. 'Dis Ray got new specs' is slightly weaker than 'Pat took a turn' because it tries harder and the logic is slightly more comprehensible, reducing the absurdity. But still very strong character comedy and benefits from the established pattern.

jokes.text: My friend In-A-Pro drives a Prius with his behind neighbor.
jokes.setup: Michael continues mnemonics, now tackling 'inappropriate behaviors'
jokes.punchline: The mnemonic has become so elaborate it now requires a Prius, a neighbor relationship, and a bizarre compound name 'In-A-Pro' — the system is collapsing under its own weight
jokes.explanation: The rule of threes pays off here. Each mnemonic has been worse than the last, and 'In-A-Pro drives a Prius with his behind neighbor' represents the system reaching full absurdist collapse. 'Behind neighbor' is a sublimely weird phrase. This is the peak of the running gag. The escalation structure is textbook-excellent.

jokes.text: Does this work for you? Yep.
jokes.setup: Michael has just delivered three increasingly absurd mnemonic devices to Jan's lawyer
jokes.punchline: Michael earnestly asks if his bizarre system works; the lawyer flatly confirms it does, which is somehow funnier than objecting
jokes.explanation: A perfect button on the mnemonic sequence. The lawyer's 'Yep' is funnier than any skeptical pushback would have been — it implies she's so desperate for Michael to be prepared that she'll validate anything. Maximum economy: two words do all the work.

jokes.text: Tell them how much you're going to get if you win. Come on, Michael, that's tacky. Million dollars. 4 million. $4 million! Man, that is a lot of guacamole! Lot of the green. Lot of green.
jokes.setup: Jan tries to stop Michael from blurting out the settlement amount by calling it tacky
jokes.punchline: Michael ignores her, announces the full amount, then celebrates it by calling it 'a lot of guacamole' — reducing a potentially life-changing legal victory to an appetizer metaphor
jokes.explanation: 'A lot of guacamole' is a genuinely funny choice — it's the specific food that makes it work. The escalation from tacky refusal to full dollar amount announcement to food metaphor is nicely structured. 'Lot of the green' doubling down makes it funnier.

jokes.text: That is why I have memorized Jan's answers and I've also thrown in some 'er's' and 'ah's' just to make it seem like it's not memorized. Perfect crime!
jokes.setup: Michael explains his deposition preparation strategy
jokes.punchline: He has memorized scripted answers but added verbal filler to disguise the memorization — and proudly calls this a 'perfect crime'
jokes.explanation: 'Perfect crime' is the joke — Michael's grandiose framing of what is obviously terrible witness coaching. The specificity of 'er's and ah's' is a great detail. This is the kind of joke that only works because Michael genuinely believes in his own cunning.

jokes.text: Hey, Schneider, real quick, what do you call a buttload of lawyers driving off a cliff? A good start. And I think it's 'busload.' Yeah, a bunch of rich lawyers took the bus.
jokes.setup: Michael attempts a classic anti-lawyer joke to break the tension with Jan's attorney
jokes.punchline: The lawyer corrects his malapropism ('buttload' vs 'busload'), and Michael's defense — 'a bunch of rich lawyers took the bus' — misses the point entirely
jokes.explanation: The meta-joke is that the lawyer corrects Michael's joke delivery, which leads to Michael defending his malapropism with a nonsensical class-commentary excuse. Michael's inability to accept correction even on a joke he's actively botching is perfect character work. The original anti-lawyer joke is a known cliché but the layer of Michael destroying it redeems it.

jokes.text: We just want to be sure that you won't do anything to hurt us with your testimony. Do you understand? Abso-fruitly.
jokes.setup: The company's lawyer gives Michael a serious, stakes-establishing request about his testimony
jokes.punchline: Michael's solemn confirmation is 'Abso-fruitly' — his signature malapropism of 'absolutely'
jokes.explanation: Michael's malapropisms are a character staple, and 'abso-fruitly' is one of the better ones — the fruit reference adds an odd whimsy. The comedy comes from the contrast between the gravity of the legal situation and Michael's childlike verbal tick. Not a landmark joke but solid and quotable.

jokes.text: Game, son! All right, let's run it back.
jokes.setup: Cold cut to the warehouse; Darryl has just beaten Jim at Ping-Pong
jokes.punchline: Darryl's trash talk is completely disproportionate to the stakes of a warehouse Ping-Pong game
jokes.explanation: Darryl's 'Game, son!' is sharp because it establishes the subplot's energy immediately. The scene cut from the serious legal drama to this is itself a comedic juxtaposition. Solid but not exceptional.

jokes.text: The warehouse got a Ping-Pong table last week. Now Jim comes down and plays with Darryl. Sometimes I bring him juice. My boyfriend is 12.
jokes.setup: Pam explains the new warehouse Ping-Pong situation with affection
jokes.punchline: 'My boyfriend is 12' — delivered as a matter-of-fact conclusion, reframing Jim's enthusiasm as childlike
jokes.explanation: Four words after a gentle two-sentence setup. 'My boyfriend is 12' is a perfect comedy sentence — unexpected, characteristically Pam in its tolerant affection, and instantly quotable. The structure is immaculate: the juice detail makes Jim seem childlike just before the punchline confirms it. One of the episode's best jokes and among the show's most quotable Pam lines. Economy score near perfect — not a single wasted syllable.

jokes.text: What has two skinny chicken legs and sucks at Ping-Pong? Hi, Kelly. Guess whose boyfriend it is? I don't want to guess. I'll give you a hint, it's not my boyfriend.
jokes.setup: Kelly delivers a riddle-format trash talk directed at Jim
jokes.punchline: She interrupts her own joke's natural answer ('Jim') with 'I'll give you a hint, it's not my boyfriend' — smugly distancing herself from the insult's target
jokes.explanation: Kelly's smug self-satisfaction ('it's not MY boyfriend') is the real joke. The insult itself is middling but the delivery and character voice are strong. Kelly using a riddle format for trash talk is very on-brand.

jokes.text: I don't talk trash. I talk smack. They're totally different. Trash talk is all hypothetical, like, 'Your mama's so fat she could eat the Internet.' But smack talk is happening, like, right now. Like, 'You're ugly and I know it for a fact 'cause I got the evidence right there.'
jokes.setup: Kelly draws a precise philosophical distinction between 'trash talk' and 'smack talk'
jokes.punchline: Her definitions are absurdly specific and delivered with academic authority — 'Your mama's so fat she could eat the Internet' as the hypothetical example, and then immediately insulting Jim's appearance as a live demonstration
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's best joke. Kelly creating a rigorous taxonomy of verbal aggression — complete with a worked example of each category — and then immediately demonstrating smack talk on Jim is writing of the highest order. The 'eat the Internet' hypothetical is perfect absurdism. The pivot to 'you're ugly and I know it for a fact 'cause I got the evidence right there' as a live demonstration is structurally brilliant. This is comparable to the anchor 8.0 example and surpasses it — it's genuinely original, perfectly structured, and absolutely Kelly Kapoor and no one else. A legitimate 9-level joke.

jokes.text: Okay, it's not regulation size, but it'll do. You have to practice. You have to get really good and beat Darryl.
jokes.setup: Pam has set up a tiny Ping-Pong table (implied by 'not regulation size') and is coaching Jim with great seriousness
jokes.punchline: The incongruity of Pam treating a novelty Ping-Pong table as acceptable training equipment for a warehouse grudge match
jokes.explanation: The visual of a tiny Ping-Pong table in the conference room is doing most of the work here, but we can only infer it from 'not regulation size.' Pam's earnestness is charming but the joke isn't especially strong on its own without the visual.

jokes.text: Your boyfriend is so weak, he needs steroids just to watch baseball. Jim couldn't hit a Ping-Pong ball if it was the size of the moon. Were Jim's parents first cousins that were also bad at Ping-Pong?
jokes.setup: Kelly continues her smack talk campaign against Jim, riffing on his Ping-Pong incompetence
jokes.punchline: Each insult escalates in absurdity — from steroid weakness to moon-sized balls to a genetics-based family insult specifically about Ping-Pong
jokes.explanation: The 'first cousins that were also bad at Ping-Pong' insult is a genuinely inventive riff — it takes the classic 'were your parents cousins' structure and adds the hyper-specific Ping-Pong qualification, which makes it absurdly funny. The steroid/baseball line is solid. Good escalation of Kelly's established smack-talk persona.

jokes.text: Toby? Are you renewing your divorce vows before my deposition? Michael, I'm your HR rep. I'm on your side. Never. I want him gone. I don't talk until he leaves.
jokes.setup: Toby appears at the deposition in his legitimate HR capacity; Michael reacts with horror
jokes.punchline: Michael refuses to participate in legal proceedings as long as Toby is present, as if Toby's presence is more threatening than the deposition itself
jokes.explanation: The Michael-hates-Toby dynamic is one of the show's most reliable running gags, and its deployment here — Michael prioritizing his irrational Toby hatred over his own legal interests — is characteristically absurd. 'Are you renewing your divorce vows' is a mean, specific insult that works perfectly. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: People underestimate Michael. There are plenty of things that he is well above average at, like ice-skating. He is a very good ice-skater.
jokes.setup: Jan gives a confessional about Michael's underestimated qualities, seemingly building to something professional
jokes.punchline: The only specific example she can produce in his defense is that he is a good ice-skater
jokes.explanation: A masterclass in structure. Jan begins with a sincere defense of Michael ('people underestimate him') that creates genuine expectation, then the only example she can muster is an irrelevant physical skill. The pause before 'like ice-skating' is everything — it implies she searched hard and that's all she found. This is both a devastating Michael burn and a revealing Jan character moment. Approaches the 8+ anchor quality.

jokes.text: Hey, Kevin, Jim needs to see you. About what? He needs help balancing some travel receipts. Are you sure he wants me? Because I have Oscar balance my travel receipts. Yeah, no, he asked for you specifically. He's in the conference room.
jokes.setup: Pam lures Kevin to the conference room under the pretense of accounting work
jokes.punchline: Kevin is flattered to be called upon for financial tasks — unaware that Oscar does his own receipts — while actually being recruited as a Ping-Pong opponent
jokes.explanation: Kevin's eagerness to be needed for accounting despite being the worst accountant in the office is good character comedy. The detail that Oscar actually does his receipts is a quiet burn. The setup for the training reveal works well.

jokes.text: Kevin enters the conference room and sees the tiny Ping-Pong table — his face lights up: 'Awesome!'
jokes.setup: Kevin has been told he's needed for accounting work in the conference room
jokes.punchline: His delighted 'Awesome!' upon seeing a Ping-Pong table instead of receipts reveals he prefers this completely
jokes.explanation: Kevin's single word of pure joy at being tricked into playing Ping-Pong is a lovely character moment. His enthusiasm for anything except work is completely consistent. The word 'Awesome!' carries tremendous weight as a reaction beat — it's the whole scene in one word.

jokes.text: Awesome! [Kevin arrives at the Ping-Pong table, clearly having been tricked]
jokes.setup: Kevin was told Jim needed him for travel receipts.
jokes.punchline: Kevin sees the Ping-Pong table and says 'Awesome!' — he's not upset at all about being deceived, he's delighted. The joke is that Kevin would rather play Ping-Pong than do his actual job, and he doesn't need convincing.
jokes.explanation: Perfect payoff to the previous joke. Kevin's immediate 'Awesome!' without any confusion or resentment tells us everything about him. One word, perfectly placed. High economy score.

jokes.text: How long have you known the plaintiff? I haven't actually seen it, but I have seen The Firm and I'm planning on renting The Pelican Brief.
jokes.setup: The lawyer asks Michael a standard deposition question about how long he's known Jan
jokes.punchline: Michael interprets 'the plaintiff' as a film title and responds with his legal thriller movie viewing history
jokes.explanation: Michael mishearing 'the plaintiff' as a movie title and responding with his legal film resumé is inspired character comedy. The specific choices — The Firm (seen it) and The Pelican Brief (planning to rent it, not seen yet) — add texture and feel completely authentic. The fact that he's using movie knowledge to prepare for a real legal proceeding is characteristically, perfectly Michael. Hits the 8.0 anchor level.

jokes.text: And you were directly under her the entire time? That's what she said.
jokes.setup: The lawyer asks a standard question about Michael's reporting relationship to Jan
jokes.punchline: Michael deploys his signature 'That's What She Said' joke in the middle of a legal deposition, completely derailing proceedings
jokes.explanation: The 'That's What She Said' joke is a running gag throughout the series, but its deployment HERE — in a formal legal deposition about his actual romantic relationship with his boss — creates extraordinary irony. The joke simultaneously works as a juvenile double entendre AND is accidentally accurate (Jan literally WAS his direct superior). The aftermath (the lawyer trying to parse who said what) elevates it further. Character integration is nearly perfect.

jokes.text: Come again? That's what she said? ... Well, delivery's all wrong. She's butchering it.
jokes.setup: The court reporter reads back Michael's 'That's What She Said' in a flat monotone, causing confusion
jokes.punchline: Michael's primary concern is not the legal catastrophe he's caused but that the court reporter's read-back has ruined the joke's delivery
jokes.explanation: This is among the episode's finest moments. The court reporter's flat monotone read-back of 'That's What She Said' destroys the joke, and Michael's reaction — 'delivery's all wrong, she's butchering it' — reveals that he is more distressed about the comedic integrity of his joke than about the legal disaster unfolding. This is profound character comedy: Michael cares more about being funny than about his girlfriend's case or his own testimony. The meta layer (a joke about a joke being delivered badly) is executed with perfect confidence. Approaches the 9+ anchor range.

jokes.text: Did Ms. Levinson ever say why she thought she was being fired? She thought it had to do with the twins. That's what I call them.
jokes.setup: Lawyer asks about Jan's beliefs regarding her termination; 'the twins' could mean colleagues
jokes.punchline: Michael reveals 'the twins' is his personal nickname for Jan's breasts, delivered as a proud clarification
jokes.explanation: The misdirection works well — 'the twins' is a natural phrase that initially implies people. 'That's what I call them' as a proud owner's clarification is cringe-comedy gold. The follow-up escalation makes it better.

jokes.text: Could you be more specific. Who are the twins? To be delicate, they hang off milady's chest. They make milk.
jokes.setup: The lawyer asks Michael to clarify what 'the twins' refers to
jokes.punchline: Michael attempts tact ('to be delicate') and produces the most clinical yet bizarre description possible — 'they hang off milady's chest. They make milk.'
jokes.explanation: 'Milady's chest' is an extraordinary phrase — pseudo-courtly language that Michael apparently believes is appropriately delicate for a legal proceeding. 'They make milk' as a separate declarative sentence, delivered flatly, is the perfect escalating punchline. The structure (attempt at delicacy → biological fact) is immaculate. This is one of the episode's truly memorable comedy moments. 'Milady' alone is worth an 8.

jokes.text: Yes. And frankly, the timing was nothing short of predominant.
jokes.setup: Michael is agreeing that Jan's breast surgery was connected to her firing
jokes.punchline: He means 'preeminent' or perhaps 'predominant' in the sense of obvious/significant, but 'predominant' is simply the wrong word used with total confidence
jokes.explanation: Michael's malapropisms are a character staple. 'Predominant' in this context is wrong but not funny enough to be a standout — it's a service joke that gets a mild laugh. Competent but not exceptional.

jokes.text: Because before we started dating, we disclosed our relationship to HR. And I have the proof right here. [long pause as Michael fumbles for document]
jokes.setup: Michael triumphantly announces he has proof of the HR disclosure — a genuine legal trump card
jokes.punchline: The dramatic pause before he produces the document implies fumbling, or the document is not where he expected — the confidence-to-scramble gap is the comedy
jokes.explanation: The comedic pause (implied by the timestamp gap) between 'I have the proof right here' and the next scene marker is a classic timing beat. Michael's theatrical confidence followed by a scramble is reliable character comedy. Primarily a visual/timing joke that loses power in transcript form.

jokes.text: If it's from the first time we kissed, it's, like, two years ago. Excuse me? If it was from the first time we kissed sober, it was, like, four months after that.
jokes.setup: Michael is asked when his relationship with Jan began; he gives a 'handshake' answer, then a kissing answer
jokes.punchline: His unprompted qualification — 'the first time we kissed sober' — reveals that there was a prior drunken kiss that doesn't count in his reckoning, devastating Jan's case
jokes.explanation: The escalating timeline reveal is beautifully constructed. Michael genuinely tries to be helpful and precise, which is why he volunteers 'the first time we kissed sober' — he's not being malicious, just thorough. This makes the cringe much deeper. The casual revelation that their relationship started drunk, framed as a helpful clarification, is peak Michael Scott self-destruction.

jokes.text: Line. I'm sorry, what? He asked for a line, like in a play.
jokes.setup: Michael, having contradicted himself under pressure, asks for a 'line' — a theatrical term for when an actor forgets their scripted dialogue
jokes.punchline: He has literally confused his deposition with a theatrical performance, treating his memorized answers as a script and the deposition room as a stage
jokes.explanation: This is a perfect callback. Earlier Michael described memorizing Jan's answers with 'er's and ah's' — a theatrical approach to testimony. Now, cornered by a contradiction, he literally asks for a 'line' as if in a play. This reveals that Michael truly sees the deposition as a performance rather than a legal proceeding. Jan's lawyer having to explain to the room that 'he asked for a line, like in a play' is the devastating coda. Excellent structure and character integration.

jokes.text: "Mr. Scott, do you realize you just contradicted yourself?" "I did." "Yes, you did." "Can I go to the bathroom?" "No." "I really have to. I've been drinking lots of water." "You went five minutes ago." "That wasn't to go to the bathroom, that was to get out of a question." "You still have to answer it." "First, can I go to the bathroom?" "No."
jokes.setup: Michael has been caught contradicting himself and the lawyer demands he address it
jokes.punchline: Michael's entire evasion strategy is a series of bathroom requests, culminating in his admission that his previous bathroom trip was also an evasion tactic — which he then immediately repeats
jokes.explanation: The escalating bathroom exchange is a masterpiece of sustained cringe comedy. The structure is perfect: (1) Michael tries the bathroom excuse, (2) it fails, (3) he explains the previous bathroom break was ALSO an evasion, (4) he immediately tries the same tactic again. The confession that his earlier escape was fake, delivered mid-escape-attempt, reveals a complete lack of self-awareness. The lawyer's increasingly flat 'No' responses are perfectly timed. This is among the episode's top three jokes and approaches the 9+ anchor territory.

jokes.text: Good game, Meredith. Don't patronize me.
jokes.setup: Jim is practicing Ping-Pong and has apparently just beaten Meredith
jokes.punchline: Meredith's genuine indignation at a congratulatory comment reveals she takes the warehouse Ping-Pong very seriously
jokes.explanation: Meredith's unexpected competitive dignity is a nice quick character beat. 'Don't patronize me' from Meredith about Ping-Pong is funny because it's disproportionate. Short and economical but not especially crafted.

jokes.text: All of my heroes are table-tennis players. Zoran Primorac, Jan-Ove Waldner, Wang Tao, Joerg Rosskopf and, of course, Ashraf Helmy. I even have a life-sized poster of Hugo Hoyama on my wall. And the first time I left Pennsylvania was to go to the Hall of Fame induction ceremony of Andrzej Grubba.
jokes.setup: Jim asks Dwight (an unexpected choice) to help him practice Ping-Pong
jokes.punchline: Dwight reveals an exhaustive and completely sincere passion for professional table tennis, naming six obscure international players and centering his entire biography around the sport
jokes.explanation: This is a perfect Dwight joke. The comedy operates on multiple levels: (1) Dwight having passionate, encyclopedic knowledge of an obscure athletic world is completely in character, (2) the names are real table tennis legends, adding absurdist authenticity, (3) 'the first time I left Pennsylvania was to go to the Hall of Fame induction ceremony of Andrzej Grubba' is a biographical statement that could only come from Dwight Schrute. The specificity and sincerity are everything. Comparable to the 8.0 anchor and above it.

jokes.text: Jan and I had an on-again/off-again relationship for two years. And I know this destroys her case and I am sorry, but I throw myself at the mercy of the deposition.
jokes.setup: Michael, in the deposition, finally admits the truth about his relationship timeline
jokes.punchline: 'I throw myself at the mercy of the deposition' — Michael conflates 'mercy of the court' with the specific proceeding type, and his theatrical surrender is both legally meaningless and somehow sincere
jokes.explanation: 'Mercy of the deposition' is a beautiful malapropism — Michael has clearly absorbed the phrase 'mercy of the court' but misapplied it to the specific procedure. His genuine regret paired with theatrical surrender is very Michael. Strong character integration.

jokes.text: What are you doing with my diary? / This is plaintiff's exhibit 107.
jokes.setup: The company's lawyers produce a document at the deposition
jokes.punchline: The document is Michael's personal diary, which Jan has secretly provided to her lawyers — the existence of which Michael had no idea about
jokes.explanation: The reveal that Jan has weaponized Michael's diary is a great plot-comedy moment. 'What are you doing with my diary?' is a line that implies Michael genuinely didn't see this coming, which is both funny and sad. Sets up the extended diary reading sequence.

jokes.text: "Just got back from Jamaica, tan almost everywhere." "Jan, almost everywhere. Hee, hee." "Oh, Diary, what a week." "I had sex with my boss. I don't know if it's going to go anywhere."
jokes.setup: Michael's private diary is read aloud in a formal legal proceeding
jokes.punchline: The diary contains a Jamaica-tan pun Michael made to himself ('Jan, almost everywhere. Hee, hee'), followed by an earnest confession about sleeping with his boss with uncertainty about its future
jokes.explanation: The diary reading is one of the episode's comedic peaks. 'Tan almost everywhere / Jan, almost everywhere. Hee, hee' — Michael made a pun in his own diary TO his diary and noted his own amusement with 'Hee, hee.' This is an act of profound creative self-satisfaction that only Michael Scott could perform. 'I had sex with my boss. I don't know if it's going to go anywhere' is devastating in its earnest uncertainty. The formality of the legal setting amplifying the intimacy of the diary entries is perfect cringe construction.

jokes.text: "Jan was very specific that this is not going anywhere, that it was a onetime mistake." "But we had sex six times, so you tell me."
jokes.setup: The diary reading continues; Michael recorded Jan's explicit statement that it was a one-time mistake
jokes.punchline: 'But we had sex six times, so you tell me' — Michael's diary logic is that frequency negates Jan's stated position
jokes.explanation: 'So you tell me' is perfect. Michael recorded Jan's explicit rejection in his diary and immediately followed it with a frequency-based counter-argument directed at the diary itself. He is arguing with his diary about his girlfriend's stated intentions. The phrasing 'so you tell me' implies he never resolved this internally — he left it as an open question for the diary to answer. Deeply funny, deeply sad, deeply Michael. Approaches 9+ anchor level.

jokes.text: "I am definitely feeling very eerie." Irie. Irie. Sorry.
jokes.setup: The lawyer reads Michael's diary phonetically; Michael wrote 'irie' (Jamaican slang for good/happy) but spelled it 'eerie'
jokes.punchline: Michael corrects the pronunciation — he used the word, spelled it wrong, and the lawyer read his misspelling literally
jokes.explanation: A nice quick laugh within the diary reading sequence. Michael used Jamaican slang in his diary (a character-revealing affectation) but misspelled it. The correction mid-reading is a light beat that works well in context.

jokes.text: "More tomorrow. X-O-X-O, Michael."
jokes.setup: The diary reading concludes
jokes.punchline: Michael signs off his diary entries with 'X-O-X-O, Michael' — sending himself hugs and kisses, in the style of a teen girl's diary or a Gossip Girl-style letter
jokes.explanation: 'X-O-X-O, Michael' is a perfect character joke in four words. Michael signs his private diary entries to himself with affectionate closings — suggesting he writes the diary as if to a pen pal, or perhaps to future Michael. It encapsulates his emotional need for warmth and validation, his complete lack of self-consciousness, and his fundamental sweetness, all in one tiny line. Economy score is near-perfect.

jokes.text: I don't think anyone in this room has a right to read my diary. / It's basic discovery. We have the right to review it. / Okay, let's make 10 copies of this diary. / Could you make it 11? / Eleven. Sure.
jokes.setup: The lawyers debate access to Michael's diary; Michael objects; the lawyers override him
jokes.punchline: One lawyer asks for 10 copies; the other requests 11 — the casual escalation implies everyone wants a personal copy, treating Michael's humiliation as a collectible
jokes.explanation: The '11 copies' request is a dark little beat — someone wants an extra copy for personal reading. Michael's privacy objection being immediately steamrolled by legal process is good cringe. The escalation from 10 to 11 implies one lawyer intends to keep their own personal copy of Michael's diary, which is quietly devastating.

jokes.text: Toby silently walks over to sit with Michael during the lunch break — Michael sees him and moves away without a word.
jokes.setup: During the lunch break, Toby approaches Michael, presumably to offer support
jokes.punchline: Michael relocates rather than sit near Toby, even during his moment of maximum vulnerability — the hatred is unconditional
jokes.explanation: A purely visual joke inferred from the transcript gap and the 'Can I sit here?' line. The fact that Michael, at his most emotionally raw moment, still cannot be near Toby, reveals that the hatred is deeper than preference — it's constitutional. The silence (Michael presumably moves without a word) is the entire joke. Strong character integration: no other character's relationship with Toby would generate this specific beat.

jokes.text: You know, I know a little bit about what you're going through in a way. When I was a kid, my parents got divorced. They both wanted custody and they both asked me to testify against the other one in court... I love them both so much. I just wanted...
jokes.setup: Toby attempts to emotionally connect with Michael during the lunch break by sharing a relevant personal story
jokes.punchline: The story — which is genuinely sad — trails off into nothing, Toby unable to finish, while Michael ignores him completely. The attempted connection is itself the joke: Toby's earnest vulnerability goes entirely unacknowledged.
jokes.explanation: This is a layered, bittersweet joke. Toby's story is genuinely sad and relatable — and completely wasted on Michael. The fact that his story trails off ('I just wanted...') without resolution, presumably because Michael has walked away or is visibly not listening, turns real pathos into dark comedy. The show does this brilliantly — Toby's sadness is always the punchline, and the punchline here is his attempt at human connection being absorbed by silence.

jokes.text: How could you give up my diary like that? / I had to. I'm sorry, but I need to win this. / How did you even find it? / You keep it under my side of the mattress. I don't like the lump.
jokes.setup: Michael confronts Jan about betraying his diary; Jan explains she found it under the mattress
jokes.punchline: 'I don't like the lump' — Jan's reason for knowing where the diary was is a domestic complaint about sleeping comfort, implying she has been suffering the lump of the diary under her side for some time
jokes.explanation: 'I don't like the lump' is a perfect understated joke — Jan's motivation for knowing the diary's location is entirely self-centered (sleep comfort), and she either hadn't read it or had read it long ago and filed it away. The mundane domesticity of 'I don't like the lump' as the reason a diary was used as a legal weapon is beautifully absurd.

jokes.text: All right, I stole your diary and gave it to my lawyer. You e-mailed a topless photo of me to everyone in our company. Let's call it even.
jokes.setup: Michael is upset about the diary betrayal; Jan counters with her own grievance
jokes.punchline: Jan's counter-grievance — that Michael emailed a topless photo of her to the entire company — is introduced casually as an equivalent exchange, and Michael accepts it
jokes.explanation: This is a stunning piece of character comedy. The casual revelation that Michael once mass-emailed a topless photo of Jan to the entire company — delivered by Jan as a negotiating chip, and accepted as fair by Michael — tells us everything about their relationship. The 'Let's call it even' frame implies both parties have been keeping moral ledgers of each other's betrayals and Michael silently agrees this is an acceptable trade. Darkly funny, perfectly calibrated, and completely specific to these characters.

jokes.text: Fine. I love you. I love you, too.
jokes.setup: Michael and Jan have just traded accusations of major relational betrayals
jokes.punchline: They immediately and sincerely exchange 'I love yous' — the emotional whiplash from mutual grievance to affection is instant and completely genuine for both of them
jokes.explanation: The immediate 'Fine. I love you. / I love you, too.' after discussing diary theft and topless email distribution is a beautiful beat. The speed of the reconciliation — no processing time, no residual anger — reveals the dysfunction at the center of their relationship with perfect economy. Four words do all the work.

jokes.text: Mr. Scott, who is this other woman, Ryan, who you refer to here as 'Just as hot as Jan, but in a different way.' / Not a woman, just a cool, great-looking, best friend.
jokes.setup: The lawyers have found Michael's diary entry describing Ryan in romantic terms
jokes.punchline: Michael's defense — 'not a woman, just a cool, great-looking, best friend' — inadvertently confirms the content of the diary while denying any romantic implication
jokes.explanation: Michael's defense of his Ryan diary entry perfectly captures his obliviousness. 'Just as hot as Jan, but in a different way' in a diary is already damning; his response — 'not a woman, just a cool, great-looking, best friend' — confirms every aspect of the quote while denying its implication. The comma between 'cool' and 'great-looking' suggests he considered the appearance compliment separately. Deeply funny character beat that reveals Michael's unprocessed feelings for Ryan.

jokes.text: Not a woman, just a cool, great-looking, best friend.
jokes.setup: The lawyer asks Michael who the 'other woman' Ryan is.
jokes.punchline: 'Cool, great-looking, best friend' as Michael's defense of why he'd describe a man this way in his diary — the 'great-looking' qualifier doing enormous work.
jokes.explanation: The defense only deepens the comedy. 'Cool, great-looking, best friend' is exactly how Michael talks about Ryan and it's exactly as ambiguous as the diary entry. The total unawareness is pure Michael.

jokes.text: All right, this is the way I see it. Yes, I had sex with Jan and, yes, I did consider Jan to be my girlfriend. However, Jan clearly did not consider me to be her boyfriend. So her actions are completely rightful.
jokes.setup: Michael attempts to bring clarity to the legal proceedings by stating his understanding of the situation
jokes.punchline: His 'clarification' is actually a devastating summary of Jan's position — she didn't consider him a boyfriend — which he concludes vindicates her, accidentally arguing against Jan's case
jokes.explanation: Michael earnestly summarizes the situation and accidentally argues against his girlfriend's wrongful termination case. 'So her actions are completely rightful' — Michael's generosity toward Jan is simultaneously touching and legally catastrophic. The comedy is that he genuinely believes he's being helpful and fair. Excellent character integration.

jokes.text: It's admirable the way you defend a woman who is so obviously ambivalent about her relationship with you. / Thank you very much. You didn't have to say that.
jokes.setup: The lawyer offers what is clearly a condescending observation about Michael's defense of Jan
jokes.punchline: Michael receives the backhanded observation as a genuine compliment and thanks the lawyer sincerely
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect irony joke. The lawyer's observation is transparently condescending — it's a legal trap and a personal dig. Michael's genuine, warm 'Thank you very much. You didn't have to say that' transforms the attack into a received compliment. The 'You didn't have to say that' adds a layer of modest deflection that makes it even funnier. Michael's inability to process sarcasm as a character trait has never been more elegantly deployed.

jokes.text: She was going through a divorce. And she was drinking a lot. / Okay. / Of water.
jokes.setup: Michael is explaining why Jan gave him bad performance reviews, mentioning her drinking
jokes.punchline: After the lawyer's skeptical 'Okay,' Michael adds 'Of water' — a desperate retroactive qualification that both reveals he knows the drinking was a problem and attempts to cover for Jan
jokes.explanation: This is the single best joke in the episode. The structure is flawless: Michael mentions Jan's drinking, receives a skeptical 'Okay' from the lawyer, and then — after a beat — adds 'Of water.' The retroactive qualifier is not only unconvincing, it makes things dramatically worse by confirming he knows the drinking was notable enough to require denial. The pause before 'Of water' is everything. Maximum economy: two words that simultaneously incriminate Jan, reveal Michael's protective instinct, and demonstrate his complete inability to manage testimony. This approaches the 9.5 anchor level in structure and economy.

jokes.text: "I am out of carrots. I am out of sticks. Mr. Scott has time and again proven himself to be an unmanageable employee and a poor branch manager. I recommend he be removed from that position and reassigned to sales where he belongs."
jokes.setup: Michael is asked to read aloud a performance review written by Jan — his girlfriend — during their relationship
jokes.punchline: The review is professionally devastating ('I am out of carrots. I am out of sticks.') and was written while they were officially dating — Jan's professional assessment of Michael as a partner is the opposite of her personal one
jokes.explanation: 'I am out of carrots. I am out of sticks.' is a magnificently despairing opening to a performance review. It implies Jan tried every management approach and found Michael resistant to all of them. Having Michael read this aloud — a review written by his girlfriend, about him, during their relationship — is perfect cringe architecture. The 'reassigned to sales where he belongs' is a particularly brutal professional put-down that doubles as a character assessment.

jokes.text: Michael reads the devastating performance review — then a long silence as the camera holds on his face.
jokes.setup: Michael has just finished reading a performance review where his girlfriend called him an unmanageable poor manager
jokes.punchline: The long silence — Michael processing what he has just read about himself, in public, written by someone who then told him 'I love you' — is the joke
jokes.explanation: The sustained silence after Michael reads the review is a master class in reaction comedy. Steve Carell's ability to hold silence and let the audience feel Michael's dawning comprehension is legendary — the joke IS the silence and what it implies about Michael learning something terrible about how his girlfriend really sees him. A purely visual/performance joke that loses almost all power in transcript form but is essential to the episode's emotional architecture.

jokes.text: How's it going? / Well, he has gone from completely hopeless to simply miserable.
jokes.setup: Pam checks in on Jim's Ping-Pong training progress
jokes.punchline: Dwight's assessment — 'completely hopeless to simply miserable' — is delivered as a genuine improvement report, implying he sees this as meaningful progress
jokes.explanation: Dwight's clinical assessment of Jim's progress as genuine improvement — 'completely hopeless to simply miserable' — is a great deadpan joke. The specificity of the scale (hopeless → miserable → ?) implies Dwight has a mental framework for athletic development that includes these states as distinct, nameable stages.

jokes.text: Check this out, though. Spin serve. Works, like, 80% of the time, so... / Nice.
jokes.setup: Jim demonstrates progress with a single advanced serve
jokes.punchline: Jim has mastered exactly one move (the spin serve, working 80% of the time) and is ready to declare himself prepared; Dwight's flat 'Nice' implies skepticism
jokes.explanation: A mild beat. Jim's overconfidence in a single move is relatable but not especially crafted. Dwight's 'Nice' is good deadpan but the scene is primarily transitional.

jokes.text: Wait a minute, Darryl is the client? / No, no, no, he works here, dumb ass!
jokes.setup: Jim has spent the episode believing he's training to defend Pam's honor against Kelly by beating 'a client'; he suddenly realizes Darryl — who works in the warehouse — was never a client
jokes.punchline: Pam's 'dumb ass' reveals she never said Darryl was a client — Jim invented the client story to justify the training, and is only now realizing it
jokes.explanation: A beautifully delayed reveal. The 'client' framing was never established by Pam — Jim invented it, or misheard, and spent an entire episode training under false pretenses. Pam's 'dumb ass' is the rare moment where the consistently sweet Pam drops the veneer and the contrast is hilarious. Strong structure — this lands as a genuine plot revelation that's also a joke.

jokes.text: Michael, I am very sorry. We never meant for you to get caught in the middle of this.
jokes.setup: Jan's lawyer apologizes to Michael privately after the performance review revelation
jokes.punchline: The lawyer who just used Michael's diary and extracted devastating admissions from him is now apologizing — her regret is about collateral damage to Michael, not about the legal tactics
jokes.explanation: The irony is clear but doesn't quite land as a joke — it's more of a tonal beat that bridges into Michael's emotional moment. The comedy is understated here, functioning more as cringe narrative than punchline.

jokes.text: Dunder Mifflin has always treated me with the utmost respect, with loyalty. / They were going to give me your job, and I should have taken it.
jokes.setup: Michael defends Dunder Mifflin's loyalty to Jan; Jan challenges this with the corporate job he was denied
jokes.punchline: Michael's instant pivot from 'utmost respect and loyalty' to 'they were going to give me your job and I should have taken it' — a two-second flip from defending the company to attacking Jan
jokes.explanation: Michael's immediate pivot from Dunder Mifflin defender to Jan attacker — triggered by one prompt — reveals that his loyalty is entirely contextual and emotional. The speed of the reversal is the joke. Good character integration.

jokes.text: Counsel: 'Mr. Wallace, regarding Michael Scott, was he a contender to replace Jan Levinson?' David Wallace: 'Yes.' [Michael reacts] 'See? I was number-one contender. I was being groomed.'
jokes.setup: Michael is confident — David Wallace confirmed he was a contender.
jokes.punchline: Michael interprets 'Yes, he was a contender' as confirmation of being the frontrunner, immediately claiming 'number-one contender' and 'being groomed.'
jokes.explanation: Strong setup for the escalating Wallace revelation. Michael's jump from 'contender' to 'number-one contender' and 'being groomed' is pure self-delusion. The joke is in the distance between the actual statement and Michael's interpretation.

jokes.text: Counsel: 'Was he your first choice?' David Wallace: 'Michael Scott is a fine employee who has been with the company many years.' Counsel: 'Was he in the top five of contenders?' David Wallace: 'What do you want me to say? Come on, he's a nice guy. There were many people that I considered.' Counsel: 'Was he being seriously considered for the corporate job?' David Wallace: 'No.'
jokes.setup: Jan's lawyer reads Wallace's deposition; Michael initially hears that he was a 'contender'
jokes.punchline: Each successive question strips away another layer of Michael's perceived status: not first choice → not top five → not seriously considered. The final 'No' after 'What do you want me to say? Come on, he's a nice guy' is devastating.
jokes.explanation: This is the episode's comedic and emotional apex. The structure is perfect: Jan deploys this as a weapon against Michael, thinking it will help her case, but instead creates a scene of almost unbearable cringe comedy. Wallace's escalating deflections — the platitude ('fine employee, many years'), the exasperation ('What do you want me to say?'), the empathy dodge ('come on, he's a nice guy'), culminating in flat 'No' — perfectly mimic the experience of being diplomatically destroyed. The comedy is in the architecture: each question removes another illusion, and Wallace's honest 'No' after trying every evasion is a masterpiece of devastating understatement. This is episode-defining comedy that approaches the show's best work.

jokes.text: I have one more question, Mr. Scott. Wouldn't you agree with Ms. Levinson that the company exhibits a pattern of disrespect toward its employees? / [long silence] / Absolutely not.
jokes.setup: Having just heard that the company never seriously considered him for promotion, Michael is asked if the company disrespects its employees
jokes.punchline: After a long silence during which the audience fully expects him to agree — given what he just heard — Michael answers 'Absolutely not,' choosing loyalty to Dunder Mifflin over his own interests and Jan's case
jokes.explanation: This is a perfect character joke and an emotionally resonant one. The long silence after the Wallace deposition reading — during which Michael presumably processes being told he was never seriously considered — creates enormous expectation. His 'Absolutely not' is both funny (he's choosing loyalty over self-interest after being publicly humiliated) and deeply revealing of Michael's character. He loves Dunder Mifflin more than he loves himself. The pause IS the joke, and 'Absolutely not' is both punchline and character revelation simultaneously. Tied with Joke 59 as the episode's pinnacle.

jokes.text: Yes! Way to go! See that? / Yeah. The floppy-haired girl you date won a point. Nineteen serving four.
jokes.setup: Jim wins a point in the Ping-Pong rematch and celebrates
jokes.punchline: Darryl's 'floppy-haired girl you date' — a deflating, gendered insult — followed immediately by the score reveal (19-4) contextualizes Jim's celebration as pathetically premature
jokes.explanation: Darryl's dismissive description of Pam ('the floppy-haired girl you date') and his refusal to acknowledge Jim's point as meaningful — the score is 19-4 — is funny and specific. 'Nineteen serving four' as a standalone beat is devastating. Strong character voice for Darryl.

jokes.text: Hey, hey, you, you / I don't like your boyfriend / 'Cause, 'cause, 'cause, 'cause / 'Cause he sucks at Ping-Pong
jokes.setup: Kelly continues her smack talk by singing a parody of Avril Lavigne's 'Girlfriend'
jokes.punchline: The Avril Lavigne parody replaces 'I don't like your girlfriend' with 'I don't like your boyfriend' and the reason is not romantic rivalry but Ping-Pong incompetence
jokes.explanation: Kelly's Avril Lavigne parody is a perfect expression of her character: she speaks in pop culture, she's simultaneously invested in pop music and workplace drama, and she deploys maximum effort on minimum stakes. The parody works because it's Kelly's most natural language. 'Cause he sucks at Ping-Pong' as the dramatic climax of an Avril Lavigne riff is genuinely funny and completely specific to Kelly Kapoor.

jokes.text: You know what? I'm sick of this. Let's go. You and me! / What? / Let's go! Pick up a paddle. / Okay. Bring it on. I am. / You think you can handle this? / In my sleep.
jokes.setup: Pam has been watching Kelly trash-talk Jim throughout the episode
jokes.punchline: Pam — who has been the supportive, mild-mannered girlfriend throughout — suddenly challenges Kelly directly; Kelly accepts with equal bravado
jokes.explanation: The reversal — Pam, the episode's gentle straight-woman, suddenly becoming the challenger — is a strong character subversion. 'In my sleep' from Kelly is perfect confidence comedy. The scene escalation from trash talk to actual confrontation is earned over the episode's Ping-Pong subplot.

jokes.text: Volley for serve. 'P.' 'O.' 'P.' 'O.'... Do you want to go play on the table upstairs? 'P.' 'O.' Yes.
jokes.setup: Pam and Kelly begin their Ping-Pong showdown with a volley for serve
jokes.punchline: The rally immediately becomes so sustained and skillful that they agree to move to the full-size table upstairs — suggesting both Kelly and Pam are secretly excellent at Ping-Pong while Jim and Darryl made a production of it
jokes.explanation: A perfect subplot resolution. The entire episode has been about Jim struggling to beat Darryl while Pam orchestrates training and Kelly trash-talks. The reveal that Pam and Kelly — the women who've been secondary to the competition — are actually so good they need to move to a regulation table is a beautiful structural reversal. The P-O exchange (a sustained rally) implies genuine skill. The joke subverts every gendered assumption embedded in the subplot and lands as both funny and satisfying.

jokes.text: Hey, David? Yeah? I think you're a nice guy, too. Thanks, Michael.
jokes.setup: Michael catches David Wallace after the deposition to deliver a message.
jokes.punchline: Michael is referencing the deposition where Wallace said Michael was 'a nice guy' while refusing to confirm he was seriously considered for the job. Michael's response to that damning evasion is to say 'I think you're a nice guy, too' — earnestly reciprocating the one small kindness in the proceedings.
jokes.explanation: This is the emotional and comedic peak of the episode's Michael/Dunder Mifflin thread. Michael's response to his most humiliating professional moment is to thank the man who delivered the blow for calling him 'a nice guy.' It is simultaneously heartbreaking and perfectly funny. The economy is flawless — 'I think you're a nice guy, too' does everything: it's a callback, a character revelation, a comedy beat, and a moment of genuine pathos. This is Michael Scott in five words. Earns high scores across the board and is the episode's most complete joke.

jokes.text: Jan said that it was because of the photo that she revealed the diary. But she already brought the diary with her to New York. So...
jokes.setup: Michael confessional, processing Jan's betrayal
jokes.punchline: Michael calmly deduces — through simple logic — that Jan had always planned to use his diary, and her excuse about the photo was retroactive cover. His 'So...' trails off, implying he's reached the conclusion but can't bring himself to state it.
jokes.explanation: The trailing 'So...' is the joke — Michael has done the math and understands he was betrayed intentionally, but the camera holds on his inability to complete the sentence. This is a sad, funny, and deeply human moment. The comedy is in the gap between what he's figured out and what he can say aloud.

jokes.text: You expect to get screwed by your company, but you never expect to get screwed by your girlfriend.
jokes.setup: Michael offers a confessional reflection on the day's events
jokes.punchline: The double meaning of 'screwed' — betrayed professionally vs. sexual — lands with Michael completely unaware of the entendre, making it an inadvertent TWSS moment from the king of TWSS
jokes.explanation: The episode's most elegant joke and its emotional capstone. Michael — who deployed 'That's What She Said' in the deposition — now inadvertently makes a double entendre about Jan without noticing. The irony is profound: the man who turns everything into a sexual joke delivers the episode's most genuinely meaningful line, which also happens to be a double entendre. 'You never expect to get screwed by your girlfriend' works as genuine heartbreak AND as an unintentional TWSS callback. This is writing at the highest level of character-integrated comedy. Rivals Joke 51 for the episode's best line.

jokes.text: What do you want to do for dinner? / How about Chinese? / We should really try to save some money. How about something cheap? / That was my cheap suggestion. Chinese was my cheap suggestion.
jokes.setup: Michael and Jan resume domestic life immediately after the emotional deposition, planning dinner
jokes.punchline: Jan's 'Chinese was my cheap suggestion' — Jan, who is suing for $4 million, is apparently calibrating 'cheap' at takeout Chinese prices — and Michael has asked for something cheaper
jokes.explanation: The return to mundane domesticity — immediately after an emotionally harrowing day — is a classic Office tonal move. The argument about whether Chinese is cheap enough is funny because of the context: these two people just had their most intimate secrets read aloud in a legal proceeding and now they're haggling over takeout price points. The 'That was my cheap suggestion' from Jan has a petulant precision to it that's very Jan.

jokes.text: What do you want to do for dinner? How about Chinese? We should really try to save some money. How about something cheap? That was my cheap suggestion. Chinese was my cheap suggestion.
jokes.setup: Jim and Pam discuss dinner after the Ping-Pong saga ends.
jokes.punchline: Jim dismisses 'Chinese' as not cheap, Pam defends it as HER cheap suggestion — the tiny domestic squabble over the relative cost of Chinese food is both relatable and funny as a couple's argument.
jokes.explanation: Sweet, low-key observational comedy. The 'Chinese was my cheap suggestion' is a realistic couple's squabble — relatably mundane. Not particularly original but lands as a warm, human beat to close the episode's B-plot.

jokes.text: Can you do fast food? / Fine. / Fast food's fine.
jokes.setup: The dinner negotiation continues; Michael suggests fast food
jokes.punchline: Jan's acceptance — 'Fine' — and Michael's echo 'Fast food's fine' with a flat tone closes the episode with two defeated people agreeing to the least romantic dinner possible after the worst day of their relationship
jokes.explanation: A quiet, perfectly deflating button on the episode. The emotional journey from 'I love you / I love you too' at the deposition to 'Fast food's fine' is a complete arc. The comedy is tonal — this is what their relationship looks like at its most honest, and it's both sad and funny. The repetition of 'fine' implies neither party is fine.

tmdb_overview: Michael is driving to New York with Jan where he is going to speak at her deposition. Jan is suing Dunder Mifflin for four million dollars over her wrongful termination. Michael is excited to testify and has memorized every answer Jan told him to.
